title: The Boy and the Heron is a disappointing mess.
summary: A 95-minute essay arguing Miyazaki's The Boy and the Heron is one of his weakest films: characters are underdeveloped archetypes serving the plot, the pacing is too fast, five themes are crammed into two hours, and the world's rules are never explained. He reads the film through Nietzsche (will to power, amor fati) and concludes it feels selfish and unmemorable despite gorgeous visuals.
claims: The Boy and the Heron is one of Miyazaki's worst films, not a masterpiece, because characters, plot and themes are all underdeveloped
Great Ghibli films build a self-contained universe with its own rules that fully makes sense by the end and leaves a clear message; this one leaves questions unresolved
Show, don't tell is a tenet of good storytelling, but Mahito's whole emotional backstory is crammed into the first 10-15 minutes, so most viewers miss it
Characters bend to the plot instead of the plot growing from the characters, which makes them feel like robots or NPCs
Kiriko and the father are empty archetypes relying on nostalgia for earlier Ghibli characters; leaning on nostalgia signals having nothing new to say
First rule of horror: never reveal the monster; turning the threatening Heron into comic relief in one scene kills all tension, unlike No-Face's film-long arc in Spirited Away
Contrary to common criticism that it is too slow, the film is far too fast; Ghibli films need contemplative 'useless' scenes that let you connect with characters
Most Ghibli films handle 2-3 themes; Boy and the Heron tries five (war, grief, creation, family, humanity) in about 2 hours, so pacing is rushed and themes go unresolved
Beautiful visuals without meaning are empty sensationalism; people remember how a film made them feel, not how it looked
Many set pieces are recycled from Pom Poko, Spirited Away, Howl's Moving Castle and The Cat Returns, getting close to Disney-style nostalgia recycling
The great-uncle is modeled on Nietzsche: trying to impose will to power to create a perfect world, a human only produces monsters, like the parakeets standing in for consumerist humanity
Mahito refusing to inherit the world and returning to reality embodies amor fati: accepting one's fate and facing life rather than escaping into artificial paradises
Escapism into artificial paradises verges on nihilism and is the surest way to an unfulfilling, miserable life; live in the present, not with ghosts of the past
As a child he could not understand why Chihiro leaves the spirit world; he now sees the message as refusing escapism
He has written a seven-page essay on the film and rewatches Mononoke and Spirited Away every year because he learns something about himself each time
His wife's theory: the uncle stands for Miyazaki himself, an aging creator with too many worlds and no successor
The film may be a warning about AI art: technically perfect but soulless visuals that will never move humans like a person with pen and paper
Even so, the film is better than 99% of Japanese animation; it only fails by Ghibli standards
